summary: Describes the Certificate Request Message Format syntax and semantics, used to ask a Certification Authority, possibly via a Registration Authority, to produce an X.509 certificate. A request typically includes a public key and registration information. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the application form for getting a digital ID card. It lists what to write: your public key and some details about you.

questions: what is proof of possession in pki
what is a certificate request message
subtitle: The message format for asking a Certification Authority to issue an X.509 certificate.

tldr.problem: Different certificate enrollment protocols all need a way to say what certificate is wanted and to prove the requester holds the matching private key. Each would otherwise invent its own request object.
tldr.mechanism: CRMF defines a CertReqMsg with a certificate template, an optional proof-of-possession and optional registration information. It is an object, not a protocol, so a separate certificate request protocol carries it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4211 obsoletes RFC 2511 and is updated by RFC 9045. It leaves transport, algorithms and registration details to the protocol that uses it.

today: RFC 4211 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2511 and is updated by RFC 9045. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What CRMF Is and Is Not
sections.content:
The Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF) is an object used to ask a Certification Authority (CA), possibly through a Registration Authority (RA), to produce an X.509 certificate. A request typically includes a public key and related registration information.

CRMF is not a stand-alone protocol. It is meant to be used by an externally defined Certificate Request Protocol (CRP), which is expected to define which algorithms are used and which registration information and controls apply. Requests may come from an RA on behalf of a subject, from a CA asking for a cross-certificate from another CA, or directly from an end entity.

Building a request takes four steps: construct a CertRequest, calculate a proof-of-possession value if required, combine these with registration information into a CertReqMessage, and communicate it securely to a CA. The means of secure transport is left to each CRP.
sections.plainLanguage: CRMF is only the form, not the post office. Some other system has to carry the form to the people who hand out the ID cards.

sections.title: The Request Message
sections.content:
A CertReqMsg has three parts. certReq is the template of the certificate being requested; not every field has to be filled in. popo is the proof that the future subject has the private key, and its shape depends on the key type and how it will be used. regInfo is optional supplementary information.

regInfo SHOULD hold only supplementary information such as contact or billing details. Data meant for the certificate content SHOULD go in certReq. But if an RA adds content to certReq, it can invalidate the proof-of-possession, so such data MAY instead be given in regInfo. A CertReqMessages value is a sequence of one or more of these messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has three boxes: what you want on the card, proof the key is yours, and extra notes for the office.

sections.title: Proof of Possession
sections.content:
Proof-of-possession (POP) lets a subject show it can use the private key matching the public key in the request. Any CRP referencing this document MUST enforce POP by some means, either in-band with CRMF or out of band. Without it, the CA cannot assume the key is really bound to the named identity.

The ProofOfPossession field is a choice of raVerified, signature, keyEncipherment and keyAgreement. With raVerified, an RA states that it checked POP itself, which it uses when the CA need not check and the RA must change the template. A requestor MUST NOT set it. If the CA requires POP, the RA MUST forward the request and proof unaltered.

Signature keys

The requester signs data containing the identity. If the template has both the public key and a subject name, the signature is computed over the DER-encoded certReq. Otherwise poposkInput is required, and carries either a sender name or a publicKeyMAC built from a shared password.

Key encipherment and key agreement keys

The requester can supply the private key encrypted (the encryptedKey choice, an EnvelopedData of type id-ct-encKeyWithID), decrypt a challenge sent by the CA/RA, or accept the certificate returned encrypted. Key agreement keys add a fourth method: a MAC (agreeMAC) made with a secret derived from the requester's private key and the CA/RA's public key. For Diffie-Hellman keys, all implementations MUST support static DH POP from RFC 2875. The thisMessage and dhMAC choices are deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write your name on a form. So you also have to show you hold the secret key, like unlocking a box only you can open.

sections.title: Password-Based MAC
sections.content:
When no authenticated identity exists yet, the requester can prove knowledge of a shared password with the id-PasswordBasedMAC algorithm. It takes a password, appends a random salt, and hashes the result repeatedly to slow dictionary attacks, then computes an HMAC. All implementations MUST support it.

Its parameters are salt, owf, iterationCount and mac. The salt SHOULD be at least 8 octets (64 bits). The iterationCount MUST be at least 100, and the RFC notes many people suggest values as high as 1000. All implementations MUST support SHA-1 as the one-way function and HMAC-SHA1 as the MAC, and SHOULD support DES-MAC and Triple-DES-MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: It mixes a secret password with some random salt and scrambles it many times, so a guesser has to do all that work for every guess.

sections.title: The Template and Controls
sections.content:
A CertRequest has a certReqId (to match a request with its reply), a certTemplate and optional controls. The template mirrors certificate fields, all optional: version, serial number, signing algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, public key, the two unique IDs and extensions.

  • serialNumber, signingAlg, issuerUID and subjectUID MUST be omitted.
  • version MUST be 2 if supplied, and SHOULD be omitted.
  • publicKey MUST be filled in if the requestor generates its own key, and is omitted if the RA/CA generates it.
  • If validity is present, at least one of notBefore and notAfter MUST be given.

The CA/RA may change any requested field except the public key, so the requestor must check the returned certificate.

Controls are attributes that are not part of the certificate but affect how it is issued. Six are defined here: regToken (one-time identity information), authenticator (long-lived, non-cryptographic identity check), pkiPublicationInfo (advisory publication wishes, which the CA/RA can ignore), pkiArchiveOptions (private key archival), oldCertID (the certificate being updated) and protocolEncrKey (a key for encrypting the CA's response). A CRP MUST define which controls it supports.
sections.plainLanguage: The template is a form where you fill in only the lines you care about. The office fills in the rest, like the card number, and can change things you asked for.

sections.title: RegInfo Controls
sections.content:
Two controls go in the regInfo field. utf8Pairs carries text name and value pairs from the subject through an RA to a CA, written as Name?Value% and repeatable. Names MUST NOT start with a numeric character, and conflicts are resolved by local policy. Appendix A lists recommended names such as corp_company, mail_email and jobTitle.

The certReq control solves a specific problem: an RA needs to change the template, but the subject used the template in its POP calculation. The RA places a new template in regInfo, copying all data from the core template. Only one such attribute is allowed, and when present the request's own template is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: If the office has to fix your form after you signed it, it staples a corrected copy to the back and uses that one instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Enrollment involves private data, so protocols must mask all subscriber-sensitive information by encryption or off-line processing. Tokens delivered out of band need protection that matches the risk the CA will tolerate. Failing to implement POP allows certificates whose public key and name do not correctly bind, enabling impersonation on signature keys and interception of encrypted messages.

Implementations must use high-entropy random number generators for keys, salts, IVs and similar values, and must protect private keys. Remote key generation should never be used for signing keys, because it undermines non-repudiation. Key escrow raises issues of identifying the escrow agent, protecting the key in transit and in storage, and returning it only to the entity that escrowed it.
sections.plainLanguage: The form holds secrets, so it has to travel in a locked envelope. A signing key made by someone else is like a signature someone else could have copied.
